article.headline: Hayek and Von Neumann Were Solving the Same Problem
article.lede: Friedrich Hayek is remembered as an economist and political philosopher, but his 1952 book *The Sensory Order* was a work of theoretical psychology — an argument that the mind constructs its representation of reality by classifying sensory inputs through a web of relationships, not by passively mirroring the world. In a recollection from an interview of unspecified provenance, Hayek described meeting John von Neumann at a party and discovering, to his delight, that the man who helped design the modern computer was approaching the same question from the same direction.
article.body:
**The Sensory Order**, published in 1952, arrived after Hayek had already become famous for *The Road to Serfdom* and was building toward the Nobel Prize in Economics he would receive in 1974. It is a work of theoretical psychology, not economics — arguing that the nervous system is less a mirror of external reality than a pattern-matching engine: stimuli are classified according to their relationships with one another, building up an internal map that mediates all perception. That almost no one he explained it to understood the project made von Neumann's instant recognition all the more striking.

Von Neumann, working from mathematics and early computing, was approaching cognition from the opposite direction. His *theory of automata* — formal systems that process inputs according to internal states, capable of self-replication and complex behavior — asked how a machine could do what a mind does. The structural overlap with Hayek's sensory classification theory is real: both frameworks describe how a complex system builds order out of incoming signals without any central designer specifying the result.

Hayek acknowledges in the quote that von Neumann's automata work, when it appeared in print, was too abstract for him to connect directly to psychology. The confession is honest and illuminating: two thinkers can triangulate the same peak from different valleys and still find the other's map hard to read up close. What they recognized in conversation — that shared angle — was the deeper intuition that minds and machines might be two instances of the same underlying logic of *information classification*.

The tweet's implicit argument is worth taking seriously. Hayek's economics already held that distributed systems encode more knowledge than any central authority can extract — the famous *knowledge problem*. *The Sensory Order* extends that intuition into neuroscience: the brain is also a spontaneous order that no designer planned. Von Neumann was building machines that could, in principle, instantiate the same logic. Together they were groping toward what cognitive science would later call the *computational theory of mind*, and they got there decades early, from opposite ends of the intellectual spectrum.

concepts.definition: Hayek's argument that the nervous system classifies sensory stimuli according to their relationships with each other, rather than representing the world directly. The result is an internal map the brain constructs through accumulated connections — an order that emerges from experience, not one imposed by any designer.

A branch of mathematics and computer science studying abstract machines that process inputs according to internal rules. Von Neumann extended this to ask how a machine could reproduce itself and perform arbitrarily complex computation, laying theoretical foundations for computer architecture and the later study of artificial life.

Hayek's argument that the information required to coordinate an economy is dispersed across millions of individuals and cannot be aggregated by any central planner. Price signals serve as the mechanism by which this dispersed knowledge is communicated without anyone needing to see the whole picture.

The philosophical position that mental processes are a form of computation — that thinking, perceiving, and reasoning can be understood as information processing governed by rules, much as a computer processes data. It became a dominant framework in cognitive science from the 1960s onward.

books.title: The Sensory Order: An Inquiry into the Foundations of Theoretical Psychology
books.author: Friedrich Hayek
books.summary: Published in 1952, this is Hayek's sustained argument that the mind organizes experience not by passively recording external stimuli but by classifying them according to a system of relationships built up through neural connections. The book draws on both philosophy and neuroscience and anticipates later ideas in cognitive science and connectionism. It is Hayek's least-read major work, sitting awkwardly between disciplines, and overshadowed by the reputation his economics built.
